questions.explanation_text: This reaction is a crossed aldol condensation. Since it occurs between benzaldehyde and acetophenone in the presence of a base, it is also called Claisen-Schmidt condensation. Benzaldehyde ( $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CHO}$ ) does not have any $\alpha$ -hydrogen. So, it cannot form an enolate ion. Acetophenone ( $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCH}_{3}$ ) has $\alpha$ -hydrogens, so the base removes one $\alpha$ -hydrogen from it. This gives the enolate ion of acetophenone: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCH}_{3}+\text{OH}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCH}_{2}^{-}+\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ The enolate ion acts as a nucleophile. It attacks the carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde, which is electrophilic. This first gives an alkoxide ion. $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CHO}+\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCH}_{2}^{-} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(O}^{-})\text{CH}_{2}\text{COC}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$ The alkoxide ion then takes a proton from water and forms a $\beta$ -hydroxy ketone. $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(O}^{-})\text{CH}_{2}\text{COC}_{6}\text{H}_{5}+\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{COC}_{6}\text{H}_{5}+\text{OH}^{-}$ This $\beta$ -hydroxy ketone easily loses water. The product formed is more stable because it has conjugation between the double bond, carbonyl group, and benzene rings. $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{COC}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\bar{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{-CH=CH-CO-C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$ So, the major product ' $A$ ' is 1,3-diphenylprop-2-en-1-one, also called chalcone. This matches option (D).

This gives the enolate ion of acetophenone:

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCH}_{3}+\text{OH}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCH}_{2}^{-}+\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

The enolate ion acts as a nucleophile. It attacks the carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde, which is electrophilic. This first gives an alkoxide ion.

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CHO}+\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCH}_{2}^{-} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(O}^{-})\text{CH}_{2}\text{COC}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$

The alkoxide ion then takes a proton from water and forms a $\beta$ -hydroxy ketone.

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(O}^{-})\text{CH}_{2}\text{COC}_{6}\text{H}_{5}+\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{COC}_{6}\text{H}_{5}+\text{OH}^{-}$

This $\beta$ -hydroxy ketone easily loses water. The product formed is more stable because it has conjugation between the double bond, carbonyl group, and benzene rings.

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{COC}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\bar{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{-CH=CH-CO-C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$

questions.explanation_text: For carbonyl compounds like aldehydes and ketones, different reagents give characteristic addition products. Hydroxylamine, $\text{NH}_{2}\text{OH}$ , reacts with aldehydes or ketones to form oximes. $R_{2}C=O+\text{NH}_{2}\text{OH} \rightarrow R_{2}C=NOH$ So, $(a) \rightarrow (ii)$ Primary amines, $R-\text{NH}_{2}$ , react with carbonyl compounds to form imines, also called Schiff bases. $R_{2}C=O+R^{'}\text{NH}_{2} \rightarrow R_{2}C=NR^{'}$ So, $(b) \rightarrow (iii)$ Alcohols, $R-\text{OH}$ , react with aldehydes or ketones in acidic medium to form acetals. So, $(c) \rightarrow (iv)$ Hydrogen cyanide, $H-C \equiv N$ or $\text{HCN}$ , adds to carbonyl compounds to form cyanohydrins. $R_{2}C=O+HCN \rightarrow R_{2}C(OH)CN$ So, $(d) \rightarrow (i)$ Hence the correct matching is: $a-ii,b-iii,c-iv,d-i$ Correct option: Option A.
questions.explanation_html:
For carbonyl compounds like aldehydes and ketones, different reagents give characteristic addition products.

Hydroxylamine, $\text{NH}_{2}\text{OH}$ , reacts with aldehydes or ketones to form oximes.

$R_{2}C=O+\text{NH}_{2}\text{OH} \rightarrow R_{2}C=NOH$

So,

$(a) \rightarrow (ii)$

Primary amines, $R-\text{NH}_{2}$ , react with carbonyl compounds to form imines, also called Schiff bases.

$R_{2}C=O+R^{'}\text{NH}_{2} \rightarrow R_{2}C=NR^{'}$

So,

$(b) \rightarrow (iii)$

Alcohols, $R-\text{OH}$ , react with aldehydes or ketones in acidic medium to form acetals.

So,

$(c) \rightarrow (iv)$

Hydrogen cyanide, $H-C \equiv N$ or $\text{HCN}$ , adds to carbonyl compounds to form cyanohydrins.

$R_{2}C=O+HCN \rightarrow R_{2}C(OH)CN$

So,

$(d) \rightarrow (i)$

Hence the correct matching is:

$a-ii,b-iii,c-iv,d-i$

Correct option: Option A.

questions.question_html:

$CH_{3}COCH_{3},CH_{3}COC_{2}H_{5},CH_{3}CHO$
questions.explanation_text: In considering the reactivity of compounds towards nucleophilic addition reactions, two primary factors need to be evaluated: the positive character of the electrophilic center and the degree of steric hindrance. Electrophilic Character : The more positive the electrophilic center, the more reactive it is towards a nucleophile. This is typically observed in aldehydes, where the electron-withdrawing effect of the carbonyl group is not counterbalanced by additional alkyl groups. Steric Hindrance : As steric hindrance increases, reactivity decreases. Larger substituents around the electrophilic center can block the approach of the nucleophile, thus lowering the reaction rate. Given these considerations, aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones due to less steric hindrance and a higher degree of positive charge on the carbonyl carbon. Between ketones, those with smaller alkyl groups are usually more reactive. Evaluate each compound based on these criteria to determine their relative reactivity in nucleophilic addition reactions.

questions.question_html: Which of the following compounds undergoes haloform reaction?
questions.explanation_text: The haloform reaction occurs when a compound contains a methyl ketone group ( $CH_{3}\text{COR}$ ) or converts into one during the reaction. Here’s a quick breakdown of each option: $CH_{3}COCH_{3}$ This is acetone, which is a methyl ketone. It has a $CH_{3}$ group directly connected to the carbonyl group. Under basic conditions with a halogen, the methyl group is transformed into a trihalomethyl group, which is then cleaved off as a haloform. Thus, acetone undergoes the haloform reaction. $HCHO$ This is formaldehyde. It lacks the necessary $CH_{3}$ group adjacent to the carbonyl (in fact, it doesn’t have a methyl group at all). Therefore, it does not undergo the haloform reaction. $CH_{3}CH_{2}Br$ This compound is bromoethane, an alkyl halide without a carbonyl group. It does not have the structure required for the haloform reaction. $CH_{3}\text{-O-}CH_{3}$ This is dimethyl ether, which is an ether and not a ketone. It does not undergo the haloform reaction. Based on this analysis, the only compound that undergoes the haloform reaction is: $\text{Option A:}CH_{3}COCH_{3}.$

Under basic conditions with a halogen, the methyl group is transformed into a trihalomethyl group, which is then cleaved off as a haloform.

Thus, acetone undergoes the haloform reaction.

$HCHO$

This is formaldehyde. It lacks the necessary $CH_{3}$ group adjacent to the carbonyl (in fact, it doesn’t have a methyl group at all).

Therefore, it does not undergo the haloform reaction.

$CH_{3}CH_{2}Br$

This compound is bromoethane, an alkyl halide without a carbonyl group.

It does not have the structure required for the haloform reaction.

$CH_{3}\text{-O-}CH_{3}$

This is dimethyl ether, which is an ether and not a ketone.

It does not undergo the haloform reaction.

Based on this analysis, the only compound that undergoes the haloform reaction is:

$\text{Option A:}CH_{3}COCH_{3}.$

questions.explanation_text: Let's analyze each option: Option A – $\text{NaBH}_{4}\text{and LiAlH}_{4}$ • Both sodium borohydride and lithium aluminum hydride are common reducing agents for ketones. • They reduce ketones by nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl carbon to form secondary alcohols. Option B – Zinc amalgam and conc. HCl • This combination is used in the Clemmensen reduction, which converts ketones (and aldehydes) into alkanes under acidic conditions. Option C – Hydrazine and KOH in ethylene glycol • This mixture is used in the Wolff–Kishner reduction, another method to reduce ketones to alkanes under strongly basic conditions at high temperature. Option D – Hydrogen in the presence of palladium on barium sulfate and quinoline • This is a poisoned catalyst (similar to the Lindlar catalyst) primarily used for the selective hydrogenation of alkynes to alkenes. • Under these conditions, ketones are not reduced. Thus, ketones cannot be reduced by the reagent listed in Option D.
questions.explanation_html:
Let's analyze each option:

Option A – $\text{NaBH}_{4}\text{and LiAlH}_{4}$

 • Both sodium borohydride and lithium aluminum hydride are common reducing agents for ketones.

 • They reduce ketones by nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl carbon to form secondary alcohols.

Option B – Zinc amalgam and conc. HCl

 • This combination is used in the Clemmensen reduction, which converts ketones (and aldehydes) into alkanes under acidic conditions.

Option C – Hydrazine and KOH in ethylene glycol

 • This mixture is used in the Wolff–Kishner reduction, another method to reduce ketones to alkanes under strongly basic conditions at high temperature.

Option D – Hydrogen in the presence of palladium on barium sulfate and quinoline

 • This is a poisoned catalyst (similar to the Lindlar catalyst) primarily used for the selective hydrogenation of alkynes to alkenes.

 • Under these conditions, ketones are not reduced.

Thus, ketones cannot be reduced by the reagent listed in Option D.
